Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Palais Lascaris, Nice, France - Museum Tour
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2659

Orientation: You are about to explore the Palais Lascaris in Nice, where a remarkable collection awaits. Encounter the Violes gambe by William Turner, the Harpe by Naderman, the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, and the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer. These works showcase the evolution of musical craftsmanship across Europe. The city of Nice's historical instruments were transferred to Palais Lascaris in 2001, culminating in the opening of a music museum in 2011, preserving and presenting these cultural treasures for all to appreciate. Your first stop is Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652). As you enter the grand salons of Palais Lascaris, let your gaze settle on the exquisite six-string bass viola da gamba crafted by William Turner in 1652. From this vantage point, the intricate carvings of the original head and pegbox become evident, showcasing Turner's mastery as a luthier.

In 2001, the Violes gambe by William Turner, crafted in 1652, was part of a significant relocation of historic instruments from the Musée Masséna to the Palais Lascaris. This transfer was driven by the city's initiative to consolidate its collection of musical artifacts within a single venue, enhancing their accessibility and preservation. As a result, the Palais Lascaris, a former aristocratic residence, now serves as a vibrant hub for musical heritage, where these instruments, including Turner's viol, are maintained in playable condition for live performances. William Turner, primarily recognized as a painter, left an indelible mark on the world of musical instruments through his viols. Operating in London, his workshop near Aldgate produced only about ten known surviving viols. This particular viola da gamba exemplifies the English approach to instrument making, featuring a bent-stave soundboard construction, a technique that offered a unique tonal quality distinct from the carved single-piece soundboards common in continental Europe. The viol's presence here at Palais Lascaris connects it to a broader narrative of European musical evolution. During the 17th century, the viola da gamba was a favorite in courtly settings, its rich, sonorous tones perfectly suited for the intimate performances of the time. This viol's journey from London's vibrant cultural scene to the aristocratic halls of Nice reflects the dynamic exchanges that shaped music in European courts. Palais Lascaris, as France's second most important collection of musical instruments, provides a fitting backdrop for this viol. The palace's commitment to preserving musical heritage ensures that Turner's viol continues to resonate with audiences today, both as a historical artifact and a living instrument. Its evolution alongside European courts highlights the changing dynamics of music as it adapted to the tastes and acoustics of different eras and venues.

Directions: Continue through Palais Lascaris — next is Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780).

Stop 2: Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2659

Orientation: To fully appreciate the elegance and historical significance of the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780), stand a few feet back to take in its full form. This position reveals the intricate carvings and gilded wood, along with the floral garlands painted on the soundboard, details emblematic of its grand past.

The harp before you emerged from Jean-Henri Naderman's workshop in Paris around 1780, a time when he crafted instruments for Queen Marie Antoinette, the last queen of France before the revolution, herself. Naderman's expertise in harp construction was widely recognized, leading to his distinguished appointment as harp maker ordinaire to the Queen in 1778. These royal connections made the harp a symbol of opulence, yet its fortune turned starkly during the French Revolution. By 1793, the harp was confiscated, illustrating the revolutionary shift away from aristocratic indulgence. Years later, this harp resurfaced in an unexpected place — the attic in the Allier department. Its rediscovery was a tangible reminder of its storied history, echoing the tumult it survived. Looking at the materiality of the harp, you'll notice its fluted column rising gracefully, supporting the neck where a single-action pedal mechanism resides. The harp's floral motifs and musical trophies hint at the sophisticated tastes of the 18th-century court, tying it back to its origins in a time of artistic splendor. As part of the broader collection at Palais Lascaris, the harp stands not just as an instrument, but as a historical artifact, bridging the gilded life at Versailles to the subdued humility that followed. It invites reflection on how music and history intertwine, the strings silent witnesses to the passing centuries within this transformed aristocratic palace.

Directions: Next: Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696).

Stop 3: Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2659

Orientation: Stand back a bit to take in the full form of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, dated 1696. From here, you can appreciate the elegant curves and finely crafted details that reflect the Italian mastery of string instruments.

In 1904, the city of Nice's collections were greatly enriched by a bequest from Antoine Gautier, a dedicated collector and musician. Among over 225 instruments he donated was this remarkable bass viol, attributed to Paolo Antonio Testore. The Testore family, known for their exquisite craftsmanship, played a crucial role in the evolution of string instrument making. Carlo Giuseppe Testore, Paolo Antonio's father, founded the family workshop in Milan, where he honed his skills under the guidance of Giovanni Grancino. This workshop, located on Contrada Larga, became a hub of innovation and artistry. The Testore family's instruments were renowned for their unique sound and enduring quality, a reputation that Paolo Antonio carried forward. Its large format and elegant design are not just visually striking but also acoustically significant. Instruments like this one were crucial in the development of Baroque music, providing the deep, resonant tones essential for orchestras of the time. Its own history, with alterations in the eighteenth century, echoes the evolution and adaptation seen in the world of musical instruments. Together, they illustrate the diverse traditions and innovations in European lutherie. As you move through this collection, consider how these instruments have shaped and been shaped by the musical narratives of their time. The Italian mastery of string instruments, exemplified by the Testore family, left an indelible mark on the musical evolution of the continent.

Directions: Your final stop in Palais Lascaris: Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581).

Stop 4: Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581)

Coordinates: 43.6954, 7.2659

Orientation: Stand near the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, 1581, and observe its elegant brass form. Here, you'll notice the craftsmanship that has preserved its original condition, a rare accomplishment for instruments of its age.

In 1901, this tenor sackbut entered the municipal collections of Nice through a bequest from Antoine Gautier, a devoted music enthusiast and collector. Gautier’s decision ensured the instrument's preservation for future generations. Originally housed at the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice, it was moved in 2001 to the Palais Lascaris, where it captivates visitors with its historical significance. Crafted in Nuremberg by Anton Schnitzer the Elder, this sackbut is remarkable for retaining its original components, including a rare brass mouthpiece, one of only four known to survive from the Renaissance period. Schnitzer specialized in producing ceremonial brass instruments, and his legacy is marked by the inscription on the bell rim, which reads, 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI.' This engraving not only authenticates the work but also highlights the craftsmanship that distinguished Schnitzer in the world of brass instruments. At the time, instruments like this represented more than musical innovation; they were symbols of cultural transformation during the Renaissance. While examining the intricate detailing of the sackbut, consider how it echoes the broader themes of the Renaissance. The artistic rejuvenation and the quest for knowledge were mirrored in musical forms breaking away from purely liturgical confines.

That's 4 stops — Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) and Confiscated in 1793, showing the shift from aristocratic luxury.
